result.paraphrase:
This article is a systematic review of research in the computing education literature on plagiarism. Its aim is to summarize the literature’s main findings and identify areas needing further study. Although there is a substantial body of work on plagiarism, no systematic reviews had been published until now.

The reviewed papers were categorized and analyzed with a Fraud Deterrence theory framework called the Fraud Triangle. In this framework, fraudulent behavior arises when a person is under pressure, sees an opportunity to commit fraud, and rationalizes the conduct in a way that makes it seem not unethical.

The review found that most papers discuss ways to reduce the opportunity to plagiarize, as well as plagiarism-detection tools. However, there is a clear shortage of empirical studies assessing how effective these deterrence strategies and tools are. The reviewed papers also mentioned many rationalizations used by computing students to justify plagiarism, especially those caused by confusion over what counts as plagiarism. Finally, research on the link between pressure in computing courses and plagiarism was found to be very limited and out of proportion to the important role this factor plays in plagiarism.
